q: What does `0 == ""` evaluate to in JavaScript, and `0 === ""`?
o: false, false
true, false
true, true
false, true
e:
`==` (loose equality) first converts both values to a common type (type coercion). The empty string becomes the number 0, and 0 == 0 is true.
`===` (strict equality) compares type AND value with no conversion: a number is never equal to a string, so false.
Coercion rules are full of surprises, so always use `===` and `!==`.
r: Always use === in JavaScript.

q: What is logged?
o: undefined
ReferenceError
null
e:
Before running code, JavaScript moves declarations to the top of their scope ('hoisting'). `var a` is hoisted and set to `undefined`; the assignment `= 1` stays where it is.
So the code behaves like: `var a; console.log(a); a = 1;` → undefined.
With `let` or `const` you would get a ReferenceError: they are hoisted too, but cannot be used before their line (the 'temporal dead zone').
r: var is hoisted as undefined; let/const throw if used early.

q: What is logged?
o: undefined x3
e:
`setTimeout` callbacks run later, after the loop has finished.
`var` creates ONE variable `i` for the whole function, shared by all three callbacks. When they run, `i` is already 3.
With `let i`, each loop iteration gets its own new `i`, so it logs 0 1 2.
r: Loops with callbacks: use let, not var.

q: In what order are the letters logged?
o: A B C D
A D C B
A D B C
A C D B
e:
JavaScript runs on one thread with an event loop:
1. First all normal (synchronous) code runs: A, then D.
2. Then the microtask queue is emptied: promise callbacks → C.
3. Then the next macrotask runs: timers like setTimeout → B.
So promise callbacks always run before timers, even timers set to 0 ms.
r: Sync code → promise callbacks (microtasks) → timers (macrotasks).

q: How do arrow functions treat `this`?
o: They bind `this` to the global object always
No own `this`; it comes from the enclosing scope
`this` is always undefined inside every arrow
They treat `this` the same as regular functions
e:
In a normal `function`, `this` depends on HOW the function is called (e.g. `obj.method()` → obj), which often breaks when you pass it as a callback.
Arrow functions don't have their own `this`; they use the `this` of the code around them. That makes them perfect for callbacks inside methods.
Don't use arrows for object methods that need `this` to be the object.
r: Arrow functions borrow this from where they are written.
fa: They have no own `this`; they capture it lexically from the enclosing scope

q: `Promise.all([p1, p2, p3])` when p2 rejects?
o: It waits for all, then returns results and errors
It rejects when p2 rejects; the others keep running
It ignores p2 and returns the other two results
It retries p2 until it finally succeeds on its own
e:
`Promise.all` runs promises in parallel and gives you all results, but if ANY of them fails, the combined promise fails immediately with that error. The others are not cancelled; their results are just ignored.
Use `Promise.allSettled` to get every result and every error, `Promise.race` for the first to finish, `Promise.any` for the first success.
r: Promise.all fails fast; allSettled waits for everything.
fa: Rejects as soon as p2 rejects (fail-fast); the other promises keep running

q: A list has 1,000 items, each needs a click handler. Best approach?
o: Attach 1,000 separate listeners, one for each item
Event delegation: one listener on the parent element
Inline `onclick` attributes written on each item
Poll the list every second to check for clicks
e:
When you click an element, the event 'bubbles' up through all its parents.
So you can put ONE listener on the list container and check which item was clicked with `event.target.closest("li")`.
It uses less memory and automatically works for items added later.
r: Many similar elements → one listener on the parent.
fa: Event delegation: one listener on the parent, use `event.target.closest(...)`

q: Search-as-you-type should call the API only after the user pauses typing. Technique?
o: Throttle
Debounce
Memoization
Polling
e:
Debounce waits until events STOP for a set time (e.g. 300 ms) and then runs once. Typing 'python' fast triggers one search, not six.
Throttle runs at most once per interval while events keep coming, good for scroll or resize handlers.
Also cancel outdated requests with AbortController so an old, slow response cannot overwrite a newer one.
r: Debounce = run after the pause. Throttle = run at most every N ms.

q: Why does React need a stable `key` on list items?
o: For the CSS styling of every item in the list
So reconciliation can match items between renders
Keys are optional; they only remove a warning
For SEO indexing of every item in the list
e:
When a list re-renders, React compares the new items with the old ones to update only what changed. The `key` tells React which old item corresponds to which new one.
If you use the array index as key and the list is reordered or filtered, React matches the wrong items: input text or checkbox state can jump to another row.
Use a stable unique ID from your data.
r: List keys = stable IDs, not indexes.
fa: So reconciliation can match items between renders; unstable keys (like array index on reorderable lists) cause wrong state and extra re-mounts

q: `useEffect(fn, [])` runs `fn`…
o: After every render of the same component
Once after mount, and cleans up on unmount
Before the first render of the component
Never, since an empty array disables effects
e:
`useEffect` runs side effects (fetching data, subscriptions, timers) after React has drawn the component.
The dependency array says when to re-run it: `[]` = only after the first render; `[userId]` = whenever userId changes; no array = after every render.
The function you return is the cleanup (unsubscribe, clear timers). In development, StrictMode runs effects twice on purpose to reveal missing cleanups.
r: Dependency array controls when an effect re-runs.
fa: Once after the component mounts (cleanup on unmount); in development StrictMode it mounts, unmounts and re-runs once to surface bugs

q: Why doesn't this re-render?
o: `useState` cannot store arrays, only primitives
The same array reference is set, so React skips it
`push` is asynchronous in plain JavaScript code
`setItems` needs to be awaited before the push
e:
React decides whether to re-render by checking if the new state is a different object than the old one.
`push` changes the existing array, so `setItems(items)` passes the SAME array, React sees no change and does nothing.
Always create a new array or object: `setItems(prev => [...prev, x])`.
r: Never mutate React state; create a new copy.
fa: The same array reference is passed; React compares with Object.is and skips the update. Create a new array: `setItems([...items, x])`

q: What does React's reconciliation do?
o: It compiles JSX to WebAssembly for the browser
It diffs old and new trees and patches the DOM
It syncs the state of components to the server
It caches the API calls that components make
e:
Changing the real DOM is slow. When state changes, React builds a new description of the UI, compares it with the previous one ('diffing') and changes only the parts of the real DOM that differ.
Rules: if an element's type changes (div → span), React rebuilds that subtree; in lists, keys identify which child is which.
r: Reconciliation = diff old and new UI, update only the changes.
fa: Diffs the new element tree against the previous one and applies minimal DOM updates

q: `useMemo` vs `useCallback`?
o: They are identical in behavior and purpose
`useMemo` memoizes a value; `useCallback` a function
`useCallback` memoizes values; `useMemo` functions
Both of them cache API responses between renders
e:
Every render re-runs your component function, recreating values and functions.
`useMemo(() => expensiveCalc(data), [data])` keeps the RESULT until `data` changes.
`useCallback(fn, [deps])` keeps the same FUNCTION object, so child components wrapped in `React.memo` don't re-render needlessly.
Use them where they help, not everywhere.
r: useMemo → value. useCallback → function.
fa: `useMemo` memoizes a computed value; `useCallback` memoizes a function reference

q: A controlled input in React means…
o: The DOM holds the value, which is read with a ref
React state is the truth, via `value` and `onChange`
The input is disabled so users cannot type in it
The value is kept in the browser's localStorage
e:
In a controlled input, React state holds the value: `<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />`. Every keystroke updates state, and state decides what is shown.
This lets you validate or format as the user types.
An uncontrolled input keeps its own value in the DOM and you read it with a ref when needed.
ec:
const [name, setName] = useState("");
<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />
r: Controlled = React state drives the input.
fa: React state is the single source of truth via `value` + `onChange`

q: With `box-sizing: border-box`, a `width: 200px` element with 20px padding and 2px border renders…
o: 244px wide
200px wide total
220px wide
180px wide
e:
Every element is a box: content + padding + border (+ margin outside).
With the default `content-box`, `width` applies only to the content, so the box is 200 + 2×20 + 2×2 = 244px.
With `border-box`, `width` includes padding and border, so the box is exactly 200px. Most projects set `* { box-sizing: border-box }` because it is easier to reason about.
r: border-box: width includes padding and border.

q: Which CSS selector has the highest specificity?
o: `div p`
`.card .title`
`#header`
e:
When several CSS rules target the same element, the more specific selector wins. Ranking: inline styles > IDs > classes, attributes and pseudo-classes > element names.
`#header` (one ID) beats `.card .title` (two classes), which beats `div p` (two elements).
If specificity is equal, the rule written last wins. Avoid `!important`.
r: ID > class > element.

q: Flexbox vs Grid?
o: Flexbox is two-dimensional; Grid is one-dimensional
Flexbox is one-dimensional; Grid is two-dimensional
They are identical in the layouts they create
Grid only works with table elements in the DOM
e:
Flexbox arranges items along ONE direction, a row or a column, and is great for toolbars, nav bars and centering things.
Grid arranges items in rows AND columns at the same time, great for page layouts and card galleries.
They are often combined: a Grid page layout with Flexbox inside each card.
r: Flexbox = one direction. Grid = two directions.
fa: Flexbox lays out in one dimension (row or column); Grid controls rows and columns together

q: `<script defer>` vs `<script async>`?
o: They are identical in how they load and run
`defer` waits for parsing, in order; `async` does not
`async` blocks HTML parsing until it has run
`defer` only works on inline scripts in the page
e:
A plain `<script>` stops the browser from reading the rest of the HTML until it downloads and runs.
Both attributes download in the background:
- `defer`: runs after the HTML is fully parsed, in the order the scripts appear. Best for your app code.
- `async`: runs as soon as it arrives, in any order. Fine for independent scripts like analytics.
r: App scripts → defer. Independent third-party scripts → async.
fa: `defer` runs after HTML parsing in document order; `async` runs as soon as it downloads, order not guaranteed

q: Which three metrics are Google's Core Web Vitals today?
o: TTFB, FCP, TTI
LCP, INP, CLS
FID, LCP, TBT
Speed Index, FCP, CLS
e:
- LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): how quickly the main content appears. Loading.
- INP (Interaction to Next Paint): how quickly the page responds to clicks and taps. Responsiveness; it replaced FID in 2024.
- CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): how much the layout jumps around while loading. Visual stability.
They affect user experience and Google search ranking.
r: LCP = load, INP = respond, CLS = stability.

q: In TypeScript, `unknown` vs `any`?
o: They are identical in behavior and in safety
`unknown` must be narrowed; `any` turns off checks
`any` is safer than `unknown` when typing data
`unknown` is only used to type caught errors
e:
`any` switches off type checking: you can do anything with it, and mistakes are only found at runtime.
`unknown` means 'I don't know the type yet': TypeScript will not let you use it until you check it, e.g. `if (typeof x === "string")`.
Use `unknown` for data from outside (JSON, API responses) and validate it.
r: Prefer unknown over any.
fa: `unknown` must be narrowed (typeof, instanceof, type guards) before use; `any` disables type checking

q: TypeScript's type system is…
o: Nominal: types match only by their declared name
Structural: types are compatible if shapes match
Dynamic: types are checked at runtime instead
Identical to the type system that Java uses
e:
TypeScript compares the SHAPE of types, not their names. If an interface requires `{ id: number; name: string }`, any object with those properties fits, even if it was never declared as that interface.
Also, types disappear when TypeScript compiles to JavaScript, so data from outside still needs runtime validation.
r: TypeScript checks shape, not name, and only at compile time.
fa: Structural: types are compatible if their shapes match

q: Which storage is sent to the server automatically with every matching request?
o: localStorage
sessionStorage
Cookies
IndexedDB
e:
Cookies are attached by the browser to every request to their domain, which is why sessions use them. They are small (about 4 KB).
localStorage (permanent) and sessionStorage (per tab) stay in the browser; JavaScript must read them and send them explicitly. Any script on the page can read them, so they are risky for auth tokens.
IndexedDB is a larger in-browser database.
r: Only cookies travel automatically with requests.

q: What is the main improvement of HTTP/2 over HTTP/1.1?
o: Headers are always sent in plain text format
Multiplexing many requests over one connection
It removed TLS support from modern browsers
It replaces TCP with a new transport protocol
e:
HTTP/1.1 handles one request at a time per connection, so browsers opened about 6 connections per site and requests waited in line.
HTTP/2 sends many requests and responses at the same time over ONE connection (multiplexing) and compresses headers.
HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (on UDP), which also avoids TCP-level waiting when packets are lost.
r: HTTP/2 = many requests in parallel on one connection.
fa: Multiplexing many requests over one connection, removing head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer

q: Why prefer `<button>` over a `<div onclick>`?
o: It is shorter and quicker to type in HTML code
Free keyboard support, focus and screen reader role
A `div` cannot be styled with CSS properties
Buttons load faster than divs in all browsers
e:
A `<button>` can be reached with Tab, activated with Enter or Space, and is announced as 'button' by screen readers, all automatically.
A clickable `<div>` does none of that; keyboard and screen-reader users cannot use it unless you add role, tabindex and key handlers yourself.
Using the right HTML element for its purpose is called semantic HTML.
r: Use real buttons, links and labels: accessibility for free.
fa: Native keyboard support, focus, and correct role for screen readers come for free

q: Main advantage of server-side rendering (SSR) over a pure client-side SPA?
o: No JavaScript at all is needed in the browser
Faster first paint and better SEO (HTML pre-rendered)
It places less load on the server than an SPA
No hydration is needed afterwards on the page
e:
In a client-side SPA, the browser first receives an almost empty HTML page, downloads JavaScript, runs it, and only then shows content.
With SSR, the server sends HTML that already contains the content, so users and search engines see it immediately. Then JavaScript 'hydrates' it to make it interactive.
Cost: more work on the server per request. Static generation (SSG) pre-builds pages at build time.
r: SSR = content visible sooner + better SEO.
fa: Faster first meaningful paint and better SEO since HTML arrives already rendered

q: What happens when you type a URL in the browser and press Enter?
a:
- The browser parses the URL; checks HSTS and its cache.
- DNS resolution: browser, OS and resolver caches, then recursive lookup → IP address.
- TCP connection + TLS handshake (or QUIC for HTTP/3).
- HTTP request with headers and cookies; it may pass a CDN, load balancer, reverse proxy, app server, database/cache.
- Response: status, headers (caching, cookies), body.
- Rendering: HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, composite; scripts may block parsing (unless defer/async); images and other resources are fetched.
- Mention where you would optimize (CDN, caching, compression, fewer round trips).

q: A web page loads slowly. How do you diagnose and improve it?
a:
- Measure first: Lighthouse, Chrome DevTools (Performance, Network), real-user Core Web Vitals.
- Network: compression (Brotli), CDN, HTTP caching, fewer/smaller requests, preconnect.
- Assets: optimize images (WebP/AVIF, correct sizes, lazy loading), code splitting, tree shaking, defer non-critical JS.
- Rendering: avoid huge DOMs and layout thrashing; reserve space for images to prevent CLS; virtualize long lists.
- Backend: slow time-to-first-byte → profile the API and database, add caching.
- Set performance budgets and monitor them in CI.

q: In a web page, what are the roles of HTML, CSS and JavaScript?
o: All three of them do exactly the same job
HTML: structure. CSS: look and layout. JS: behavior
HTML is styling; CSS is logic; JS is content
Only JavaScript is needed to build a web page
e:
Think of a house:
- HTML is the structure: walls, rooms, doors. Headings, paragraphs, buttons, forms.
- CSS is the decoration: paint, furniture placement. Colors, fonts, spacing, layout.
- JavaScript is the electricity: things that react. Clicks, fetching data, updating the page without reloading.
r: HTML = what, CSS = how it looks, JS = what it does.
fa: HTML = structure and content; CSS = appearance and layout; JavaScript = behavior and interactivity

q: In modern JavaScript, `let` vs `const`?
o: They are identical in every way in JavaScript
`const` cannot be reassigned; `let` can be
`const` objects cannot be modified in any way
`let` creates a global variable in all cases
e:
`const total = 5;` means the variable `total` cannot point to another value later. `let count = 0; count = 1;` is allowed.
Both exist only inside the `{ }` block where they are declared.
Careful: `const` does not freeze objects. `const user = {}; user.name = "Ana";` works; only `user = other` is forbidden.
Rule of thumb: use `const` by default, `let` when you must reassign, and avoid `var`.
r: const by default, let when it changes, never var.
fa: `const` cannot be reassigned; `let` can. Both are block-scoped

q: What is the DOM?
o: A database that stores the content of the page
A tree of objects built from the HTML (editable)
A CSS framework used for building page layouts
A server that sends HTML files to the browser
e:
The browser reads the HTML text and builds the Document Object Model: a tree where each tag is a node (document → html → body → div → button...).
JavaScript changes the page by changing this tree, e.g. adding an element or changing its text, and the browser redraws what changed.
r: DOM = the live tree of the page that JS manipulates.
fa: The tree of objects the browser builds from the HTML, which JavaScript can read and change

q: What does `document.querySelector(".btn")` return?
o: All of the elements that have the class btn
The first match of `.btn`, or null if none
The one element whose id is btn in the page
A string with the HTML of that one element
e:
`querySelector` accepts any CSS selector and returns the FIRST matching element, or `null` if nothing matches.
`querySelectorAll` returns ALL matches as a list.
`.btn` means class 'btn'; `#btn` would mean id 'btn'.
r: querySelector = first match. querySelectorAll = all matches.
fa: The first element matching the CSS selector `.btn`, or null if none

q: What does this do?
o: It clicks the button immediately on page load
It registers a function that runs on every click
It deletes the button from the page when clicked
It logs a message once, when the page loads
e:
`addEventListener(eventName, callback)` tells the browser: 'when this event happens on this element, call this function'.
The function is a callback: you give it to the browser, and the browser calls it later, once per click.
Other common events: "input", "submit", "keydown", "scroll".
r: addEventListener = run this function when that happens.
fa: Registers a function that runs every time the button is clicked

q: What is the result of `[1, 2, 3].map(x => x * 10)`?
o: undefined
e:
`map` calls the function on each element and returns a NEW array with the results; the original is unchanged.
`forEach` also calls the function on each element, but returns undefined; use it only for side effects like logging.
Related: `filter` keeps elements where the function returns true; `reduce` combines everything into one value.
r: map → new array of results. forEach → nothing returned.

q: What is a React component?
o: A CSS file with styles for the pages of the app
A reusable UI piece, usually a function returning JSX
A database table for storing the state of the UI
A server route that returns HTML for the pages
e:
React apps are built from components, like Lego blocks: `<Header />`, `<ProductCard />`, `<Button />`.
A component is a function that returns JSX, HTML-like syntax describing what to show. React calls it again whenever its data changes and updates the screen.
r: Component = function that returns UI.
fa: A reusable piece of UI, usually a function that receives props and returns JSX

q: In React, props vs state?
o: They are the same thing under two different names
Props are inputs from the parent; state is internal
State comes only from the server, never from users
Props can only be strings, never objects or numbers
e:
Props are like function arguments: the parent passes them, the child reads them but must not change them.
State is the component's own memory (`useState`). When you update it with the setter, React re-renders the component with the new value.
If the child needs to change something, the parent passes a function as a prop (e.g. `onChange`).
r: Props = given by the parent. State = owned and changeable.
fa: Props are inputs passed from the parent (read-only for the child); state is data the component owns and can change, triggering a re-render

q: What does this CSS do?
o: It always hides the sidebar on every screen size
It hides the sidebar on screens up to 600px wide
It makes the sidebar exactly 600px wide on screens
It hides the sidebar only on large desktop screens
e:
A media query applies its CSS rules only when a condition is true, here: the viewport is at most 600px wide (phones).
This is the basis of responsive design: one page that adapts its layout to different screen sizes.
Many teams write mobile styles first and add `min-width` queries for larger screens.
r: Media queries = CSS that depends on screen size.
fa: Hides the sidebar only when the screen is 600px wide or narrower

q: In CSS, what is the difference between `.btn` and `#btn`?
o: There is no difference between the two selectors
`.btn` targets a class (many); `#btn` an id (one)
`#btn` targets only the button elements of a page
`.btn` is not a valid selector in modern CSS
e:
A class (`.`) is a reusable label: many elements can share `class="btn"`.
An id (`#`) should identify exactly one element per page.
For styling, classes are preferred: IDs have very high specificity, which makes them hard to override later.
r: . = class (many), # = id (one).
fa: `.btn` targets elements with class="btn" (can be many); `#btn` targets the element with id="btn" (should be unique)

q: What is a Promise in JavaScript?
o: A guaranteed value that is available right away
An object for a value that arrives later, or an error
A special type of loop that is used for async code
A CSS animation that waits for events on the page
e:
Operations like `fetch(url)` take time. Instead of freezing the page, they immediately return a Promise: a placeholder for the future result.
A promise is pending, then becomes fulfilled (with a value) or rejected (with an error).
You handle it with `.then(...)` / `.catch(...)` or, more readably, with `await` inside an async function.
r: Promise = placeholder for a future result.
fa: An object representing a value that will be available later (or an error), from an async operation like a network request

q: What does `await` do inside an `async function`?
o: It blocks the whole browser until the request ends
It pauses this function until the promise settles
It turns the request into a synchronous request
It retries the request until it finally works
e:
`await` waits for a promise and gives you its value, so async code reads top to bottom like normal code.
Only THIS function pauses; the browser keeps handling clicks, animations and other code meanwhile.
If the promise rejects, `await` throws, so wrap it in try/catch to handle errors. Note: an async function itself always returns a promise.
r: await = pause this function, not the page.
fa: Pauses this function until the promise settles, without freezing the rest of the page

q: How do you request data from an API in modern JavaScript?
o: `fetch` gives a Promise; `await` it and check `res.ok`
`fetch` throws an error on every HTTP error status
`res.json()` gives the data right away, no `await`
`fetch` can only be used to load HTML documents
e:
`fetch(url)` sends an HTTP request and returns a Promise for a Response object.
Important detail: it only rejects on network failure. A 404 or 500 still resolves, so you must check `res.ok` (or `res.status`).
`res.json()` is also asynchronous, it reads and parses the body, so it needs `await`.
To send data: `fetch(url, { method: "POST", headers: {"Content-Type": "application/json"}, body: JSON.stringify(data) })`.
r: fetch does not reject on HTTP errors: check res.ok.
fa: `fetch` returns a Promise; `await` waits for it; `res.json()` parses the body; you must check `res.ok` because fetch does not reject on 404/500

q: What do `package.json` and `npm` do?
o: `package.json` lists dependencies; `npm` installs them
`npm` is a database in which packages are stored
`package.json` compiles Java code for the backend
`node_modules` is a Git branch with the packages
e:
Node.js projects (React, build tools) use npm (Node Package Manager), like Maven for JavaScript.
`package.json`: name, version, `dependencies` (needed to run), `devDependencies` (build/test tools) and `scripts` (`npm run build`, `npm test`).
`npm install` downloads libraries into `node_modules` (do not commit it) and records exact versions in `package-lock.json`. Alternatives: yarn, pnpm.
r: package.json = manifest. npm install = download dependencies.
fa: `package.json` lists the project's metadata, scripts and dependencies; `npm` is the tool that installs them into `node_modules`

q: What does a bundler such as Vite or webpack do?
o: It bundles files for the browser, with a dev server
It runs the database that the app depends upon
It replaces the browser that the users install
It writes the tests of the app for the developers
e:
Browsers cannot run JSX or TypeScript, and loading hundreds of small files is slow.
A bundler follows imports from your entry file, transpiles the code, minifies it, splits it into chunks and outputs optimized static files.
During development it serves your app and refreshes it instantly when you save (hot module replacement). Vite is the modern default for React; webpack is older; Create React App is deprecated.
r: Bundler = turns your source into optimized browser files.
fa: It combines and optimizes many JS/CSS/image files (and converts JSX/TypeScript) into a few files the browser can load efficiently, and offers a dev server with hot reload

q: In React, how should you update an array stored in state?
o: Option B: make a new array, so React sees a change
Option A: mutate the array and set the same one
Both options work in exactly the same way in React
Neither option works in React for arrays in state
e:
React decides to re-render by comparing the old and new state with `===`. If you mutate the same array (`push`) and pass it back, the reference is identical, so React may skip the update.
Always create a new value: `[...items, x]`, `items.filter(...)`, `items.map(...)`; for objects `{ ...user, name: "Ana" }`.
Treat state as immutable.
r: State is immutable: copy, don't mutate.
fa: Option B: create a new array; React detects a new reference and re-renders

q: When do you use React Context?
o: To share a value like a theme without prop drilling
To store the data of the application on the server
To style the components of the application with CSS
To run the tests of the components of the app
e:
Prop drilling means passing a prop through many intermediate components that do not use it, just to reach a deep child.
Context lets a provider component make a value available to any descendant that calls `useContext`.
Good for rarely changing, app-wide data (theme, locale, logged-in user). For complex or frequently changing global state, libraries such as Redux Toolkit, Zustand, or server-state tools like TanStack Query are often used.
r: Context = shared value without prop drilling.
fa: To share values like the current user or theme with many components without passing props through every level (prop drilling)

q: What is `useRef` for?
o: A mutable value or DOM node that does not re-render
To store state that triggers a re-render of the UI
To fetch data from an API when the component loads
To define the CSS styles of a component in React
e:
`useRef(initial)` returns an object `{ current: ... }` that React keeps between renders. Changing `current` does NOT re-render.
Uses: focusing an input (`inputRef.current.focus()`), storing a timer id, remembering the previous value, any mutable value that is not part of what the screen shows.
If the screen must update when the value changes, use `useState` instead.
r: useRef = persistent box, no re-render on change.
fa: Holding a mutable value or a reference to a DOM element that persists across renders without causing a re-render when it changes

q: What is a Single Page Application (SPA) and how does client-side routing work?
o: One HTML page; JS swaps the view and URL, no reload
A site that is made of one single file on a server
A page that is built without using any JavaScript
A page that reloads completely on every single click
e:
In a traditional multi-page site, each link asks the server for a new HTML page. In an SPA (React with React Router, Angular, Vue), the first load brings the app; afterwards the router changes the URL with the History API and renders another component, with no full reload. Data comes from REST/JSON APIs.
Benefits: fast, app-like feel. Drawbacks: larger first load, SEO and initial-render concerns (solved by SSR or static generation, e.g. Next.js).
The server must send `index.html` for unknown paths so deep links work.
r: SPA = one page, JS swaps views, data from APIs.
fa: The browser loads one HTML page and JavaScript; navigation changes the view and URL (History API) without a full page reload, fetching data from APIs as needed

q: What does this print?
e:
The chain runs step by step:
- `filter(n => n % 2 === 0)` keeps even numbers: [2, 4].
- `map(n => n * 10)` multiplies each: [20, 40].
- `reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0)` adds them starting from 0: 20 + 40 = 60.
These three array methods (filter, map, reduce) never change the original array; they return new values.
r: filter keeps, map transforms, reduce combines.

q: What is a closure in JavaScript, and what does this log?
o: 3: the inner function remembers its outer `n`
0: each call starts again from zero every time
undefined: `n` is not visible outside of it
1: only the first call changes the value of n
e:
A closure is a function that keeps access to the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that outer function finished.
`counter()` returns an arrow function that still sees its own private `n`. Each call increments the same variable: 1, 2, then 3. No outside code can touch `n` directly (data privacy).
Closures power callbacks, event handlers and React hooks.
r: Closure = function + remembered variables.
fa: 3: the inner function remembers `n` from where it was created

q: What is the difference between Angular, React and Vue at a high level?
o: React is a library; Angular is a full framework
They are all databases used to store web data
They are all CSS libraries for styling web pages
React is a backend language used to build servers
e:
All three build interactive UIs from components.
- React (Meta): library; JSX; large ecosystem; flexible, so teams pick router, state and build tools.
- Angular (Google): full framework in TypeScript with opinions: modules/standalone components, dependency injection, router, HTTP client, forms.
- Vue: approachable, template-based; the core is small, official router and store.
For an interview, know components, props, state, hooks and how to call a REST API.
r: React = library. Angular = full framework. Vue = middle.
fa: React is a UI library focused on components (you choose routing and state tools); Angular is a full framework (TypeScript, DI, router, forms built in); Vue is a progressive framework in between

q: Name a common way to test React components.
o: Jest or Vitest with React Testing Library
Only manual testing carried out in the browser
Maven Surefire, run from the backend project
Selenium only, used for every kind of test
e:
Jest or Vitest runs tests and provides assertions and mocks. React Testing Library renders components and lets you find elements like a user would (`getByRole`, `getByText`) and trigger events (`userEvent.click`).
Principle: test what the user sees and does, not internal state or implementation details.
End-to-end tests in a real browser use Selenium, Playwright or Cypress.
r: Jest/Vitest + React Testing Library for components; Playwright/Selenium for E2E.
fa: Jest (or Vitest) with React Testing Library, which tests behavior the way a user sees it

q: How would you connect a React front end to a Spring Boot REST API?
a:
- Spring side: `@RestController` returning JSON; configure CORS for the front-end origin (or serve both from the same origin); secure with Spring Security (JWT or session cookies).
- React side: call endpoints with `fetch` or axios inside `useEffect` or a data library (TanStack Query) and keep results in state.
- Handle three states: loading, error, success; check `res.ok`.
- Auth: send the token in the `Authorization` header or use `HttpOnly` cookies.
- Dev: Vite dev server proxy to `localhost:8080`; Prod: build static files and serve behind the same domain or a CDN.
- Contract: agree on DTOs and error format; consider OpenAPI (springdoc) to generate typed clients.

q: What is the frontend of a web application?
o: The part that runs on a server and stores data
The part users see and use in a browser or app
The marketing team of the company that builds it
The database that stores the application data
e:
A web application has two sides.
The frontend (also called the client side) is everything that runs on the user's device: layout, colors, buttons, forms, and the code that reacts when you click.
The backend is the other side. It runs on a server that you never see directly.
A frontend developer builds what people see and touch.
r: Frontend = what the user sees and touches.
fa: The part users see and interact with in their browser or phone: pages, buttons, forms

q: What is a web browser?
o: A search engine such as Google or Bing online
A program like Chrome that requests and shows pages
A type of server that hosts websites for others
A programming language that is used for the web
e:
A browser is an app on your device. When you type an address, it sends a request to a server, gets back HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and draws the page for you.
In client/server words, the browser is the client.
A search engine (Google, Bing) is just a website that you open with a browser.
r: Browser = the app that fetches and shows web pages.
fa: A program (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) that requests web pages from servers and displays them

q: Which sentence correctly describes HTML?
o: A programming language that does calculations on the server
A markup language for the structure and content of a page
A database format for web data
A language for colors and fonts
e:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) uses tags such as `

` (heading) or `

` (paragraph) to tell the browser what each piece of content is. It describes structure and content. Looks are CSS and behavior is JavaScript. Example: `

Hello

` is a paragraph element that contains the text Hello.
r: HTML = structure and content of the page.
fa: A markup language that defines the structure and content of a web page: headings, paragraphs, links, images

q: What does CSS control in a web page?
o: The look: colors, fonts, spacing and layout
The connection to the database of the website
Which server answers the request of the browser
The login system of the site and its users
e:
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is a language of style rules applied to HTML.
Example: `p { color: blue; font-size: 18px; }` makes every paragraph blue and bigger.
Without CSS, a page still works but looks plain. With a different CSS file, the same HTML can look completely different.
r: CSS = how the page looks.
fa: The presentation: colors, fonts, spacing and layout

q: JavaScript and Java: how are they related?
o: JavaScript is a lighter, simplified version of Java
Different languages; the similar name is historical
They are the same language with two different names
JavaScript can only run inside of Java programs
e:
Despite the name, they are not related.
JavaScript was created to add behavior to web pages in the browser. Today it also runs on servers (with Node.js).
Java is a general-purpose language that is very common in backend and enterprise systems.
In an interview, mixing them up is a red flag, so keep them separate in your head: Java is not JavaScript.
r: Java and JavaScript are different languages.
fa: They are two different programming languages with different purposes; the similar name is historical and causes confusion

q: What is the difference between a static and a dynamic website?
o: Static sites have no images, while dynamic ones do
Static serves fixed files; dynamic builds per request
Static sites need a database; dynamic sites do not
There is no real difference between the two kinds
e:
Static site: the server just finds a file (for example `about.html`) and sends it as it is. Everyone sees the same content.
Dynamic site: the server runs code, reads data (for example from a database), fills an HTML template and sends a page built for that request. A shop showing your orders is dynamic.
Static sites are simpler and cheaper. Dynamic sites are more flexible.
r: Static = same files for all. Dynamic = built per request.
fa: A static site sends the same ready-made files to every visitor; a dynamic site builds each page on request, often with data from a database

q: Where does client-side code run, and where does server-side code run?
o: Both run on the server, never in the browser
Client-side runs in the browser; server-side on a server
Client-side runs in the DB; server-side in the browser
Both run in the billing system of a cloud provider
e:
Client-side code is downloaded to the user's device and runs there: for example the JavaScript that opens a menu when you click.
Server-side code runs on a server you control. It receives requests, talks to the database, checks permissions, and builds the response.
Anything on the client can be seen and changed by the user, so important checks (security, prices) must be repeated on the server.
r: Client-side = in the user's browser. Server-side = on your server.
fa: Client-side runs in the user's browser or app; server-side runs on a server, which receives requests and sends responses

q: What is Node.js?
o: A database used for storing web application data
A JavaScript runtime to run code outside the browser
A CSS framework used for building page layouts
A cloud provider that rents out servers by the hour
e:
JavaScript was born inside browsers. Node.js is a program that can run JavaScript code on any computer, so you can write a backend or a script in JavaScript.
Node.js describes itself as a free, open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime environment, built to be asynchronous and event-driven.
A runtime is the program that executes your code.
r: Node.js = JavaScript outside the browser.
fa: A JavaScript runtime that lets you run JavaScript outside the browser, for example to build servers and command-line tools

q: What is React?
o: A database that is used for web applications
A JavaScript library to build UIs from components
An operating system that runs on web servers
A testing tool that is used for Java projects
e:
React's own website calls it 'the library for web and native user interfaces'.
You build a page from components: pieces of UI with their own logic and appearance. A component can be as small as a button or as large as a whole page.
React components are JavaScript functions that return markup written in JSX, a syntax that looks like HTML.
r: React = components for building UIs.
fa: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components

q: What is TypeScript?
o: A faster version of Java made for the browser
JavaScript with types, compiled down to plain JS
A CSS preprocessor that adds variables and nesting
A query language used for relational databases
e:
In JavaScript, a variable can hold anything and mistakes appear only while the program runs.
TypeScript adds types, for example `let age: number = 30;`. The TypeScript compiler catches mistakes (like using a string where a number is expected) before you run the code.
The result is converted to normal JavaScript, which is what browsers and Node.js run.
r: TypeScript = JavaScript + types.
fa: JavaScript with added type annotations; it is checked before running and then compiled to plain JavaScript

q: What is the difference between UI and UX?
o: They are two names for exactly the same thing
UI is what you see; UX is the whole experience
UI is for mobile apps; UX is for desktop apps
UI is the code of the app; UX is the hardware
e:
UI is the visible surface: buttons, text, layout.
UX is how the product feels to use: can people find what they need quickly, do they make mistakes, do they get frustrated?
A beautiful screen (good UI) can still have poor UX if the steps are confusing.
r: UI = what it looks like. UX = how it feels to use.
fa: UI (user interface) is what you see and use: screens, buttons, colors. UX (user experience) is the whole experience of using the product: how easy, clear and pleasant it is

q: Explain frontend and backend to a non-technical person.
a:
- Use the restaurant picture: the dining room is the frontend (what the customer sees and touches: menu, table, plates).
- The kitchen is the backend (where the work and the ingredients are, hidden from the customer).
- The waiter who carries orders between them is the API.
- Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript running in the browser.
- Backend: code on a server (Java, Python, Node.js...) plus a database that stores the data.
- A full-stack developer works on both sides.
